cards.a: Networking is the practice of connecting two or more computing devices so they can exchange data, share resources, and communicate. A network is defined not by the number of devices but by the ability to transmit and receive information between endpoints using agreed-upon standards and protocols.

cards.q: What business value does networking provide?
cards.a: Networking enables resource sharing (files, printers, compute, storage) and communication (email, voice, video, web) between endpoints regardless of their physical location.

cards.q: What five elements does a network need to function?
cards.a: Endpoints/hosts, transmission media, intermediary devices, protocols, and addressing. Endpoints originate or consume traffic, media carries signals, intermediary devices move or secure data, protocols define formatting and delivery, and addressing (MAC/IP) lets data reach its destination.

Connecting heterogeneous devices, addressing and naming so packets reach the right destination, path determination/routing across multiple networks, reliability and error recovery, security, and management and monitoring.

cards.q: How does layering solve networking problems?
cards.a: Each layer has a specific job and hands work to the layer below or above via encapsulation, adding headers/trailers as data travels down and removing them as it travels up at the receiver.
Communication in one direction only, for example broadcast TV or legacy one-way sensors.

cards.q: What is half-duplex communication and what is a common example?
cards.a: Communication that can occur in either direction but not simultaneously, such as walkie-talkies or legacy hub-based Ethernet.

cards.q: What is full-duplex communication and what uses it?
cards.a: Communication in both directions simultaneously, used by modern switched Ethernet and fiber.

cards.q: What is the difference between a network and the Internet?
cards.a: A network is two or more devices exchanging data via agreed standards, while the Internet is a network of networks interconnected by routing and peering. A network can be as small as two devices; size is not part of the definition.

cards.q: Why is modern Ethernet full-duplex considered an exam-relevant point?
cards.a: Half-duplex and full-duplex are frequently tested; modern Ethernet is full-duplex, while hub-based (legacy) Ethernet is half-duplex.

cards.q: What is encapsulation in the context of layered networking?
cards.a: Adding headers (and trailers) to data as it descends the layers, and removing them as it travels up at the receiver. It is needed by every protocol in this course.

cards.q: What do intermediary devices such as switches, routers, firewalls, and APs do?
cards.a: They forward or secure data; they rarely originate or consume traffic themselves.

cards.q: On Windows, what command displays IP, MAC, and default gateway information?
cards.a: ipconfig /all. On Linux/macOS the alternative is ip addr.

cards.q: Which commands verify connectivity and show the path packets take?
cards.a: ping verifies connectivity to a destination, and traceroute (tracert on Windows) shows the path packets take.
